story:
He was not in a recording studio when the sound first took shape. He was in a different kind of room, watching a film unfold. Frank Ocean was in the soft glow of 2016, finishing a visual album called Endless, a single steady shot of a carpenter building a staircase while songs and silences threaded through the hours. The piece that would open and close that film did not begin with him. It began in a kitchen in Germany, where Wolfgang Tillmans, a photographer who thinks in images and sounds, recorded a seven minute and thirty second piece on his phone. Tillmans sat at his counter and spoke aloud the very language the world uses to sell us its small bright rectangles, the press release phrases of Apple, Samsung and Sony, and he let those lines fold into a rhythmic, robotic chant that made the ordinary sound uncanny. That moment, a voice recorder, a kitchen table and a private, playful improvisation, is where the work was born.

The adventure that carried that kitchen recording into the long slow film happened with modest, human hands. Tillmans made a rough version and played it for Kyle Combs in New York, and Kyle answered by harmonizing with the vocal modulations, shaping the little vocal hollows that become an intro. Back in Berlin, Tim Knapp at Trixx Studios helped Tillmans lay the words out in a grid and create the strange time warps and cuts that make the voice feel like machinery and mirror. The track was never a sample of anything else. It was Tillmans original, recorded in one go and then refined so the voice could breathe in electronic space. Frank Ocean did not write or sing these lines. He asked to borrow a short piece of the work, fifteen seconds to set the doorway of his visual album, but then chose to let the whole seven minute composition close the film as well. So the track, titled Device Control, came into the Endless world not as Frank Ocean’s creation but as a kind of guest, a sharp bright object that bookends the carpenter and the songs within.

At the center of that sound is a clear, satirical eye. The voice reads aloud phrases lifted from the makers of our devices, and because the words are earnest sales pitches, when they repeat without the cheer and with modulations they begin to sound like commands. Tillmans said he was thinking about our addiction to devices and how we live through broadcasting and depiction. The piece holds that idea like a lantern in a fog, neither sermon nor joke, simply an observation turned into a texture you can feel. To listeners who enter Endless, the track reads like a mirror; the robotic cadence catches you by surprise and then makes you aware of how often you ourselves become the ones repeating market promises back into the world. To Frank Ocean’s film it provides a framing: opening, it asks us to notice how mediated our lives are, and closing, it leaves the echo of that noticing in the room with us.

There is a gentle strangeness to this truth. The song is both critique and lullaby; it sounds like the voice of a machine and like someone trying on a sales pitch to see how hollow it feels. It is a small performance about big habits. Those who hear it remember the tiny origination of the piece, the kitchen and the phone recorder, and they feel how easily the profound can come from a casual moment. The people who worked on it, Kyle Combs harmonizing in New York, Tim Knapp shaping time warps in Berlin, gave the piece its shape, but its center remains Tillmans speaking the words and letting their repetition do the work.

Why does this matter? Because art sometimes arrives by way of unexpected hospitality. Frank Ocean made room in his visual album for a voice not his own, and that generosity let a short, sharp critique of our device culture reach a wider audience. The track lingers because it is honest and because it sounds like the world we recognize, amplified until it is almost theatrical. It stays with people because it asks nothing less than for them to listen and to feel a little exposed by what they hear. That feeling might sting, but it also opens toward a clearer seeing. In that way the piece is hopeful, not because it fixes anything, but because it holds up a small, bright mirror and lets us, for a moment, look at ourselves and perhaps change how loudly we speak.
